title: Your own shipwreck
hook: almost everyone has a Zeno moment, a loss that became a door

segments.voice: Yesterday, parables: tell it plainly, then stop. Your line was pass it on.

Ask people how they ended up where they are, and listen for a certain kind of answer. Well, I got laid off, and that's how I found this work. Well, the engagement ended, and that's when I moved here. Well, I got sick, and it changed everything. Not every story goes that way, but some do. Somewhere in the middle there's a wreck, and on the other side of it, a door nobody would have chosen to walk through. Back on day twenty-five we met the man whose wreck became a whole school of thought.
screen: `HOW DID YOU END UP HERE?` → `WELL, I GOT LAID OFF.` → `A WRECK, THEN A DOOR.`

segments.voice: Remember Zeno: a merchant from Citium, on Cyprus, about thirty years old, sailing toward the harbor of Athens with a cargo of purple dye. The ship went down. The cargo was gone. He wandered into the city, sat down in a bookshop, and heard the bookseller reading aloud about Socrates. He asked where men like that could be found, and at that moment a philosopher named Crates walked by. The bookseller said: follow that man. Zeno did. Years later he was teaching in the painted porch, and the school took its name from it: the Stoics. The ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius tells us Zeno later said, more or less: I made a good voyage when I was shipwrecked. On day twenty-five your line put it this way: I sailed well when I was wrecked. Now the honest part, because this path doesn't do greeting-card wisdom. Not every loss becomes a door. Some losses are only losses. Nobody gets to tell a grieving person their grief was a gift, and you don't have to tell yourself that either. Zeno said it about his own wreck, years later, looking back, not the day the ship went down. But for some people there's at least one wreck that, looking back, turned out to be the way somewhere. Not good. Not deserved. But the way. In the Stoic way of seeing, the lost cargo isn't a blessing; the cargo was never the point. What mattered was what Zeno did next.
screen: `ZENO'S CARGO GOES DOWN.` · `A BOOKSHOP, AND CRATES.` · `A GOOD VOYAGE WHEN WRECKED.` · `NOT EVERY LOSS IS A DOOR.` · then, large: `THE WRECK WAS THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Gently, and only if it's there, think of one loss that, looking back, led somewhere, and compose three short lines in your head: what went down, what door it opened, where you are now because of it. If nothing fits yet, that's honest too: keep line one, and leave the other two blank for now. If you like, put the lines on paper later.
Zeno. The loss in his own story that, looking back, became a door: his sunken cargo that became a school. Today's word.
Your line: the wreck was the way. Only ever said looking back, and nobody needs rushing toward the door. That's day ninety-four.

screen: `DAY 94 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SAY WHERE IT CAME FROM.`

howItsDone: Readers of the Stoics often tell Zeno's shipwreck as a reminder that a loss can become a turning point, and some write their own turning points down, as today's practice suggests.

fork.setup: you're Zeno. your ship and your cargo are gone, and you're alone in Athens. you wander into a bookshop. what happens?
options: you sell your last coin for passage home
you hear about Socrates and ask where to find such men
you open a dye shop in the market
fork.reveal: he hears the bookseller reading about Socrates and asks where such men are. Crates walks by: follow that man. the Stoic school begins there.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything happens for a reason.
what it means: some losses, looking back, became the way somewhere; not all, and none need to be called good.
what a scholar hears: Diogenes Laertius 7.2–5, which gives more than one version of Zeno's saying about the wreck.

notes: Diogenes Laertius 7.2–5 paraphrased: confirm the cargo of purple (from Phoenicia), wreck near the Piraeus, age about thirty, the reading of Xenophon's Memorabilia book 2, Crates passing by.
Zeno's saying ('I made a prosperous voyage when I suffered shipwreck') is paraphrased; Diogenes Laertius records alternative versions. The script notes more than one version in the trapdoor.
This day handles loss; the script explicitly says not every loss becomes a door, and offers a blank-lines option in the practice.
